Your Admin

This is Boston — a city in Massachusetts. Here is where it stands today: each measure’s level, its rank among US places, and the places most like it.

Boston is home to 673,458 people, the 25th largest of 9,593 US places, and its residents earn an average salary of $106,267. The typical home is worth $972,529, and 3.8% of its labor force is out of work. The places most like it — the closest on population, density, wage, home value and share of metro — are Washington DC, Oakland, Long Beach and Cambridge. Switch the view to comparison to set each figure beside the metro’s, the peers’ and the national average.

Your Metro

The administrative city is one piece of a larger machine. People commute, firms hire, and housing supply responds across a region far wider than the city line — the labor market. We approximate it with the Metropolitan Statistical Area. Boston sits inside the Boston MSA, and most of what follows is read at that scale.

The Boston MSA holds 5,025,517 people, the 11th largest of 387 US metros, and pays an average salary of $114,779, the 5th highest. The typical home is worth $717,120, and 3.7% of its labor force is out of work. Its closest peer metros, by population, density, wage and home value, are Washington, Seattle, San Diego and Denver; the comparison view sets each figure beside theirs and beside the national average.

A metropolitan statistical area is how the US Census draws the functional city: a dense core plus every surrounding county tied to it by commuting. It is the closest official shape to the real labor market — the area within which people can change jobs or homes without changing lives.

Boston’s metro spans 197 cities and towns and about 4.9M people; the administrative city is one of them, home to roughly 13% of the metro’s residents. That is why most of what follows is read at the metro scale.

Admins in your metro

Boston is one of many places inside the Boston MSA. How much of the metro is it — its share of the region’s people and its wage bill — and how does it rank against the metro’s other places? It holds 24.8% of the metro’s people and 19.9% of its wage bill, the largest shares of any place in the region, on an average salary a little under the metro’s own.

What does the metro do for a living?

2.3 million jobs across 877 industries. Professional & business services and education & health are the two largest sectors, each about a quarter of the jobs, and trade & transportation holds another sixth. The single largest industry is general hospitals, at 5.4% of all jobs, then full-service restaurants at 4.6% and colleges and universities at 3.7%.

Complexity rank, 2024

Complexity measures the knowledge an industry takes to run. Work that needs many people holding many different specialized skills — medical devices, financial engineering, research instruments — is complex. Work that almost anywhere can do — food service, retail, basic construction — is not.

It matters because complex work is hard to copy. Places that hold it tend to pay more, to weather downturns better, and to find it easier to move into the next complex thing, because the know-how is already in the room. A metro’s complexity is the mix of its industries weighted by how much of each it does.

    How tradable is the metro’s work?

    The same blocks, now sorted into three tiers by how much of what they make can be sold outside the metro. Most of the metro’s work does not sell outward. Local work — restaurants, grocers, family services — is 49% of jobs, and another 28% is partly traded. Only 23% is traded, and that is the part bringing new income in.

    Each industry is placed in a tier by how much of what it makes can be sold to someone outside the metro.

    Traded
    sells most of its output outside the metro, so its earnings are new income arriving here
    Partly traded
    sells some outside and some to the people already here
    Local
    serves the people already here; the customer has to be standing there

    The tiers are cuts on a continuous measure, so an industry near a cut could fall the other way.

    Which tradable industries is the metro most specialized in?

    The metro is most concentrated in fabric coating mills, 12 times the national rate, then R&D in biotechnology at 10.8 and guided missile and space vehicle parts at 10.3. Concentration is not size: fabric coating mills reach 12 times on 600 jobs, while biotechnology R&D employs 62,000 at 10.8 — the one industry that is both.

    An industry counts as a specialization when the metro does more of it than the country does. The measure divides the industry’s share of jobs here by its share of jobs nationally: 1.0× is exactly the national rate, 2.0× is twice as concentrated here as anywhere else.

    It says nothing about size. A small industry can be a powerful specialization and a large one can be entirely ordinary — this measures what is distinctive about the metro, not what employs the most people.

    One city, two workforces

    Two counts sit behind every city. The jobs inside the boundary, whoever fills them, and the jobs its residents hold, wherever those jobs are. In most places the two are close. In Boston they are not.

    Start with the jobs. 687,736 sit inside the city line. Each dot is about 2,000 of them.

    Two counts sit behind every city: the jobs inside its line, whoever fills them, and the jobs its residents hold, wherever those are. In Boston the two are far apart. The map shows where the difference goes: teal arrows bring workers in, orange arrows carry residents out to their jobs.

    Only one in four of those workers lives here

    179,122 of the jobs are held by Boston residents, and those dots stay put. The other 508,614 move out to where their holders live, elsewhere in the metro.

    Its residents commute out too

    Residents hold 334,026 jobs. 154,904 of them are outside the city, and those dots now leave in orange.

    The two colours side by side are the exchange: for every resident who commutes out, more than three people commute in.

    Two workforces

    Sorted into rows, the same dots give the two counts. Jobs located here are the grey and teal rows together: 687,736. Jobs held by residents are the grey and orange rows: 334,026.

    That is 206 jobs for every 100 its residents hold. The city is a net importer of workers, and the beats that follow ask which work the two groups do.

    The work that happens in Boston

    The bigger of the two counts first: the jobs inside the boundary, filled by residents and commuters alike. Health care is the largest at 21%, then professional services at 15%, then education and finance.

    Bars are ranked by jobs located here and hold that order for the next two beats, so a sector never moves. Only what is measured about it changes.

    What Boston’s residents do

    The narrow bar is the second count: the jobs residents hold, wherever those jobs are. It sits inside the wide bar almost everywhere, which is the commuter surplus read sector by sector.

    The gaps carry it. Finance and insurance has 3.4 jobs here for every resident who works in the field. Manufacturing and management of companies are the only two where the narrow bar runs past the wide one.

    What the city does more of than its metro

    A mix on its own says little, because most places look like the region around them. The same rows now show each sector’s share of the city against its share of the metro.

    Finance and insurance is 1.9× the metro’s share. Retail, construction, wholesale and manufacturing sit well below parity: the metro does them, the city mostly does not. The hollow marks repeat the reading for residents, and they cluster near 1× — the specialisation belongs to the workplace, not to the people who live here.

    Each sector’s share of the city’s jobs, divided by its share of the metro’s. 1× means the city leans on that sector exactly as much as the metro does; 2× means twice as much.

    The city is part of the metro it is measured against, so a place this large is pulled toward parity. Read the distance from 1×, not the raw figure.

    Who it trades workers with

    Both directions on one map. Teal arrows bring workers in; orange arrows carry residents out to their jobs. Width is the number of jobs.

    Cambridge is the one near-even exchange: 24,509 residents work there and 20,085 Cantabrigians work here. Everywhere else the teal arrow wins. Quincy sends 20,328 in and takes 6,015 back.

    Workplace, or dormitory?

    Every sector above collapses into one number: jobs located here for each job a resident holds in that field. Above 1× the city imports that sector’s workers; below it, the city sends them out.

    Pick a sector to see where it lands against the city as a whole, which sits at 2.06×.

    The work that happens in Boston

    Two bars for every sector: the jobs inside the boundary in teal, the jobs residents hold in orange. Health care is the largest at 21% of the jobs here. The orange bar is shorter almost everywhere, and the gap is the commuter surplus — except in manufacturing and management of companies, where it runs past.

    What Boston does more of than its metro

    Most places look like the region around them; what separates them is where the shares differ. Each bar runs from the line where the city’s share matches the metro’s: finance is 1.9× it, retail and construction well under. Compare what residents do and the bars draw in — the specialisation is the workplace’s.

    Your City’s Most Specialized Industries

    Of the tradable industries above, these are the ones Boston does an unusual amount of. Each is measured against the national benchmark: a score of 1.0 means the industry takes up the same share of jobs here as it does across the country. Anything higher means the city is more concentrated in it than the country is — and the further past 1.0, the more distinctive it is.

    The same measure, now set against four cities of similar size and economic make-up. The tick on each row is the average of those four — where Boston’s mark runs past it, the city is more specialized in that industry than its peers; where it falls short, less. Hover any row to see the cities behind the average.

    The same measure, now read against every US metro at once — the teal dot is where the Boston metro lands. Hover any mark for the city and figures behind it.

    Take the share of your city’s jobs that sits in an industry, then divide it by the share of jobs that same industry holds nationally. Economists call the result revealed comparative advantage, or RCA.

    If an industry is 4% of jobs in your city and 1% of jobs nationally, the score is 4.0 — four times more concentrated here than in the country at large. A score of 1.0 means exactly average, and below 1.0 means the industry is thinner here than it is elsewhere.

    A high score doesn’t automatically mean a big industry — it means a distinctive one. Employment is carried in the row tooltip, and in the dot form by the size of each dot.

    Switch to Compare with peers above to hold the same scores against four metros in a similar position.

    In this view each peer is scored exactly the same way against the same national benchmark, and the tick on every row is the average of those four. Comparing against the country at large mostly tells you that Boston is a large, wealthy city; comparing against metros in the same position tells you something you can act on.

    Hover any of the four to see how it stacks up against Boston:

    Hovering a row in the chart shows each city individually, so you can see whether the average reflects the whole group or is being pulled by one outlier.
